Introduction
Two GPS systems,
one complete picture

Wellington United Diamonds use two GPS tracking systems simultaneously: Catapult and StatSports. Because different players wear different devices, the two systems track entirely different groups of players within the same match — there is no overlap, and no reconciliation between systems for the same individual is required or possible.

This report consolidates both datasets into a single unified view per game, with consistent metrics presented for every player regardless of device. Where metrics differ in definition between systems — particularly acceleration, deceleration, sprint, and high intensity distance — this is noted clearly throughout and the figures should not be directly compared across systems.

This is the definitive end-of-season report, covering all 19 fixtures from 04 April to 29 August 2026. It reconciles three record sources so nothing is misrepresented: the official match lineups (who played, and for how long), the GPS units (physical data, where a unit was worn), and the league golden-boot table (official goals). The result is a complete appearance-and-minutes matrix for all 31 players used across the season, individual analysis for every GPS-tracked player, and full game infographics.

An important finding from this reconciliation: GPS units were not worn in every appearance, so the GPS data alone understated how much several players featured — most notably Hannah Pilley, the league’s 30-goal top scorer, who played 18 games but was GPS-tracked in nine. The matrix shows tracked and untracked appearances distinctly. The season also included two Kate Sheppard Cup ties (09 and 29 May) alongside the 17 league fixtures.

Catapult  ·  provides Player Load and detailed speed zone data
StatSports  ·  provides native High Intensity Distance and High Speed Running data
Data methodology
How the data
was processed

Raw GPS exports require processing to produce accurate, comparable per-game figures. GPS devices continue recording before and after match time, so raw session totals overstate actual playing time and distance. The pipeline below converts raw exports into accurate match-time-only figures for every player in every game.

Playing-time formula: A half counts as played if Distance ≥ 800m AND Distance/min ≥ 25m/min. Catapult data is extracted from 1st-half and 2nd-half game splits (never the "all" split, which includes warm-up); StatSports from the Total session row, cross-checked against half rows.

High Intensity Distance (HID) — new this report: StatSports provides a native High Intensity Distance field, which is used directly. For Catapult, the equivalent is computed as the sum of Speed Zones 4 and 5 (the high-speed bands). Because the two systems use different underlying speed thresholds, StatSports HID reads systematically higher than Catapult HID for comparable efforts — the two should not be directly compared across systems, only within a system across games and players. HID per minute (HID ÷ minutes played) is also provided as a time-normalised intensity measure.

Distance per minute: both systems provide this natively; it is surfaced prominently as the fairest cross-game work-rate comparator, since it normalises for how long each player was on the pitch.

Playing-time & participation reconciliation: This report reconciles three sources. Official match lineups are the authoritative record of who played and for how long — every starter and substitute, with on/off minutes. GPS units (Catapult and StatSports) provide physical data, but not every player wore one every game, so GPS covers a subset of actual appearances. The golden-boot table supplies official league goal tallies. Minutes come from the lineup (or GPS where lineup detail is thin); physical metrics come only from GPS and are labelled as such; a player who took the field without a unit appears in the record with minutes but no distance. Two games are Kate Sheppard Cup ties (09 May, 29 May) — goals in these do not count toward the league golden boot. The 23 May Miramar fixture had a Catapult export bug (half durations reconstructed) and the 29 May cup tie went to extra time, so their figures are indicative.

Metric definitions: High accelerations/decelerations — Catapult: efforts ≥2 m/s²; StatSports: all recorded events (not directly comparable). Player Load is Catapult-only.

Season themes
Squad-level
insights

Hannah Pilley won the league's Golden Boot with 30 goals. The reconciliation with official lineups revealed that the team's most important attacker had been badly under-represented in the GPS-only data — she played 18 of 19 games, not the nine her GPS record showed, and her 30 league goals were the most in the entire Women's Central League. Farina Anchico added 15 (second in the squad, top three in the league), with Kennedy Corkin and Jemma Robertson on 9 each. As a team, that is a formidable spread of goal threat.

Three players were ever-present. Kennedy Corkin, Marla MacInnis and Farina Anchico each played all 19 games. Kennedy was the only one GPS-tracked in every game; the other two each missed a unit once. Together they formed the physical backbone of the squad, each logging over 1,600 minutes of on-pitch time.

GPS coverage was partial — the lineup record is the true picture. Across the season, players took the field 61 times without a GPS unit fitted. Some players were affected far more than others: Hannah Pilley (9 untracked games), Molly Simons (10), and Natalie Brook (5) all played substantially more than their GPS data alone would suggest. The appearance matrix below shows this explicitly — blue for tracked games, orange for played-but-untracked — so physical data is never mistaken for the full participation record. Sophie Flood, the goalkeeper, played six games but was tracked only once.

The load-management story holds, and is now precisely documented. After a congested early and mid-season including a 120-minute cup tie, the run-in shows Kennedy Corkin substituted off in the majority of the final seven games, and Farina rested at points too — the deliberate management the mid-season data had called for. The squad also refreshed itself throughout: Kyra Morgan and Molly Simons arrived in late May, Ela Jerez and Maddie O'Farrell in June, and Sarah Alder became a regular from July.
